article_title: Giving Mechanical Engineers Intelligent Tools: A Project-Based AI Education Curriculum in Thermal Engineering
citation: Changgen Li, Han Hu, Christy Dunlap, Nathaniel House, and Jonathan Wai. (2025). Giving Mechanical Engineers Intelligent Tools: A Project-Based AI Education Curriculum in Thermal Engineering. https://github.com/hanhuark/machine-learning-for-engineers
title: MLME: an open-access, project-based AI curriculum for thermal engineering totaling 39.1 hours with four core projects and three optional projects
description: The Machine Learning for Mechanical Engineers (MLME) course at UARK integrates AI into thermal engineering for ME students, distinct from computer-science AI courses by focusing on selection and implementation of AI algorithms for thermal problems. The article states the course is "organized into a timeline format ... totaling 39.1 hours, and covers various topics such as linear regression, multilayer perceptron (MLP), convolutional neural networks (CNN), and time series analysis." Four assignment projects cover heat flux prediction (MLP, GPR), pre-/post-CHF image classification (CNN), unsupervised PCA/SVD clustering, and RNN time-series prediction of vapor fraction; three extra projects and student-proposed projects serve as final-exam options. Syllabus, data, and code are released in open-access repositories.
requirements: Preferred entry requirements are one semester of calculus, linear algebra fundamentals, basic probability/statistics, familiarity with MATLAB or Python, and at least one thermal sciences course; high-school level mathematics and physics is the minimal prerequisite because skills are taught within the course
target_learners: mechanical engineering undergraduate and graduate students
target_learning_goals: develop, train, and test ML models using Python (TensorFlow) and MATLAB
apply ML to thermal engineering problems such as boiling monitoring, diagnosis, and prediction
NACE professional competencies including critical thinking, communication, teamwork, technology, leadership, and professionalism
examples: Project 2 requires students to train CNNs to classify pre-CHF and post-CHF boiling images and report confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, ROC, and AUC
Project 4 requires an RNN to forecast vapor fraction of future frames from past frames, varying input and output sequence lengths
key_sources: Changgen Li, Han Hu, Christy Dunlap, Nathaniel House, and Jonathan Wai. (2025). Giving Mechanical Engineers Intelligent Tools: A Project-Based AI Education Curriculum in Thermal Engineering. https://github.com/hanhuark/machine-learning-for-engineers

article_title: Giving Mechanical Engineers Intelligent Tools: A Project-Based AI Education Curriculum in Thermal Engineering
citation: Changgen Li, Han Hu, Christy Dunlap, Nathaniel House, and Jonathan Wai. (2025). Giving Mechanical Engineers Intelligent Tools: A Project-Based AI Education Curriculum in Thermal Engineering. https://github.com/hanhuark/machine-learning-for-engineers
title: Five-level pyramid hierarchy for AI-integrated engineering curricula based on scaffolded instruction
description: The MLME course is organized as a pyramid representing scaffolded instruction, in which guidance is gradually reduced as students gain mastery. The article states the course "is a project -based course designed according to the principles of scaffolded instruction [44], i.e., gradually reducing guidance as students gain mastery, which is represented as a pyramid in Fig. 2." The levels are, from the base: curiosity and self-motivation as the foundational attitude; foundational STEM knowledge provided just-in-time within each project; an introduction level teaching core ML theories and techniques; an application level practicing algorithms on publicly available datasets; and an advanced level covering thermal theory topics and the four integrative projects.
requirements: Foundational STEM knowledge must be provided before more complex concepts, with basic matrix operations and programming syntax introduced in the first project and later material given just-in-time aligned with the problem at hand
target_learners: mechanical engineering students with limited AI and programming background
target_learning_goals: progressive mastery of ML concepts and their application to thermal engineering problems
examples: In each project module, students first recognize the limits of conventional physics-based methods, then see AI-based solutions compared against them, then try simple accessible examples
key_sources: Changgen Li, Han Hu, Christy Dunlap, Nathaniel House, and Jonathan Wai. (2025). Giving Mechanical Engineers Intelligent Tools: A Project-Based AI Education Curriculum in Thermal Engineering. https://github.com/hanhuark/machine-learning-for-engineers

article_title: Effects of Mathematics Anxiety and Mathematical Metacognition on Word Problem Solving in Children with and without Mathematical Learning Difficulties
citation: Lai Y, Zhu X, Chen Y, Li Y (2015) Effects of Mathematics Anxiety and Mathematical Metacognition on Word Problem Solving in Children with and without Mathematical Learning Difficulties. PLoS ONE 10(6): e0130570. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0130570
title: Interventions for mathematical learning difficulty should address anxiety during the mathematics learning process and build metacognitive self-image
description: The article recommends that support for children with MLD target learning-process anxiety and metacognition rather than only cognitive deficits: "helping MLD children reduce anxiety during the mathematics learning process should be incorporated into future interventions." It also suggests one benefit of mathematical metacognition may be promoting beliefs about, and self-efficacy for, MLD children's mathematical abilities. The study's mediation and group-difference findings provide the empirical basis for this recommendation.
requirements: Interventions should be informed by assessment of learning mathematics anxiety (LMA) and self-image, since these distinguished MLD children from LA, TA, and HA peers in the study.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional; the authors state SEM does not warrant causal claims, and the small number of MLD students calls for caution in interpreting mediating effects in MLD children.
target_learners: Children with mathematical learning difficulty (MLD) in elementary school
target_learning_goals: Word problem solving
Mathematics achievement
Reducing anxiety during mathematics learning
examples: The study compared four mathematics achievement groups (MLD, LA, TA, HA) on metacognition and anxiety with IQ partialled out, and found MLD children's LMA higher and self-image lower than TA and HA peers.
key_sources: Lai Y, Zhu X, Chen Y, Li Y (2015) Effects of Mathematics Anxiety and Mathematical Metacognition on Word Problem Solving in Children with and without Mathematical Learning Difficulties. PLoS ONE 10(6): e0130570. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0130570

article_title: English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra
citation: Xiaojuan Ke · Kristie J. Newton. (2024). English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra. Instructional Science (2024) 52:831–858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09668-6
title: MLS-WEPs: Modified for Language Support-Worked Example Pairs supplemental algebra curriculum
description: MLS-WEPs is a supplemental curriculum for English learners adapted from Durkin and colleagues' WEP materials, in which students compare side-by-side worked examples across four types: "Which is better?", "Why does it work?", "Which is correct?", and "How do they differ?". Language supports include sentence frames, rephrased prompts of adjusted language complexity, requiring mathematical examples before conceptual answers, and allowing native-language discussion and drafting with final products in English.
requirements: Teachers received a three-hour orientation implementing the materials as if they were students, plus weekly communication with researchers
constraints: Implemented as a supplement after topics were introduced, within five unit types (Linear Equations, Functions, System Equations, Polynomials, Radicals)
target_learners: English learners in secondary sheltered algebra classes, English proficiency levels 1-5
target_learning_goals: Algebraic problem solving and calculation
Written mathematical explanation
Mathematical literacy in listening, reading, writing, and speaking
examples: Teachers implemented the Linear Equation and Function units in a crossover design, with the control group receiving the same examples with the same language supports but without comparison
key_sources: Xiaojuan Ke · Kristie J. Newton. (2024). English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra. Instructional Science (2024) 52:831–858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09668-6

article_title: A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables
citation: Julian F. Lohmann, Nils Machts, Jens Möller, Steffen Zitzmann. (2025). A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10029-z
title: A multilevel latent variable model (ML-LVM) of judgment accuracy that represents rank, level, and differentiation components as raters' latent abilities
description: The article introduces the ML-LVM, in which each rater's judgments are modeled with a rater-specific bivariate normal distribution whose mean, variance, and covariance parameters correspond to the level, differentiation, and rank components of judgment accuracy. The three components follow a multivariate normal distribution across raters, so the model yields both population-level means and variances quantifying between-rater differences. The authors note that in a traditional two-step approach, person-specific scores 'are calculated in the first stage for each teacher separately and then treated as observed variables in subsequent analyses,' which the ML-LVM avoids by accounting for sampling error from a limited number of judgments. Estimation uses Bayesian MCMC in Stan.
requirements: A benchmark vector of judgments and corresponding criterion scores (e.g., test scores or simulated student ability) for each rater
Bayesian MCMC estimation in Stan, since random variances and covariances cause estimation problems in frequentist estimation
constraints: Variance components for the benchmark can be fixed to zero only when all raters judge identical stimuli; both variance components can be fixed to zero when all raters are provided with the same judgment stimuli
target_learners: teachers and pre-service teachers whose judgment accuracy is being assessed
target_learning_goals: assessment competence (diagnostic competence): accurate teacher judgments of student characteristics such as cognitive ability or performance
examples: In the illustrative scenario, 20 teachers each evaluate 30 students; teacher A's class mean of 70 versus a population mean of 60 is captured by the random intercept uj, and an average rank correlation of 0.55 versus teacher A's 0.45 illustrates the rank component
key_sources: Julian F. Lohmann, Nils Machts, Jens Möller, Steffen Zitzmann. (2025). A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10029-z

article_title: A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables
citation: Julian F. Lohmann, Nils Machts, Jens Möller, Steffen Zitzmann. (2025). A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10029-z
title: Easy-to-use R code and step-by-step tutorial for applying the ML-LVM judgment accuracy model
description: The article states that 'Easy-to-use R code is provided to simplify the application of the new judgment accuracy model,' and Appendix 1 presents 'a step-by-step tutorial on how to apply the ML-LVM in R.' The model is estimated in the Bayesian environment of Stan using MCMC, with normal priors for intercepts and component means, half-Cauchy priors for population-level variances, and a Lewandowski–Kurowicka–Joe prior for random-effect covariances. The analysis code and dataset for the first empirical application are available on an OSF repository.
requirements: Bayesian estimation environment (Stan) with MCMC sampling
constraints: Runtime was up to 270 min per dataset in the largest sample size condition of the simulations (three chains run in parallel)
target_learners: researchers studying teacher judgment accuracy who wish to apply the ML-LVM
target_learning_goals: assessment and modeling of teacher judgment accuracy components
examples: The tutorial in Appendix 1 walks through applying the ML-LVM to the pre-service chemistry teacher dataset, including comparing results with PS-method calculations
key_sources: Julian F. Lohmann, Nils Machts, Jens Möller, Steffen Zitzmann. (2025). A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10029-z

article_title: Algorithmic Fairness in Automatic Short Answer Scoring
citation: Nico Andersen, Julia Mang, Frank Goldhammer, Fabian Zehner. (2025). Algorithmic Fairness in Automatic Short Answer Scoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00495-5
title: Eight-stage machine-learning pipeline for automatic scoring with stage-specific bias vulnerabilities
description: The article describes a machine-learning pipeline for automatic short-answer scoring comprising eight stages: data collection, scoring/labeling, preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, data split, model training, and model evaluation. For each stage it names a characteristic bias vulnerability, e.g. unrepresentative samples create "representation bias", human labeling creates "annotation bias", and unstratified data splits can induce "sampling bias". It is used to explain where unfairness can enter automatic scoring systems before it surfaces at model evaluation.
requirements: Data collected representatively with respect to demographic characteristics
Scoring according to precise scoring guidelines
constraints: Statistical models can be difficult or impossible to reconstruct and understand, especially with many interdependent parameters as in deep learning
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate automatic scoring of constructed reading-comprehension responses
examples: The article walks through each pipeline stage with a concrete bias example, such as text-length features disadvantaging boys who tend to write shorter texts in reading comprehension tasks
key_sources: Nico Andersen, Julia Mang, Frank Goldhammer, Fabian Zehner. (2025). Algorithmic Fairness in Automatic Short Answer Scoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00495-5

article_title: ML4STEM Professional Development Program: Enriching K-12 STEM Teaching with Machine Learning
citation: Jingwan Tang, Xiaofei Zhou, Xiaoyu Wan, Michael Daley, Zhen Bai. (2023). ML4STEM Professional Development Program: Enriching K-12 STEM Teaching with Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00292-4
title: ML4STEM: a two-session professional development framework for integrating machine learning into K-12 STEM teaching
description: ML4STEM is a professional development framework that prepares K-12 STEM teachers to use machine learning as a scientific discovery tool. It is "composed of two sessions: Teachers-as-Learners (TaL) and Teachers-as-Designers (TaD)", grounded in the TPACK framework with focus on TK, TCK, TPK, and TPCK, and operationalizes five principles: "learning by design, hands-on experience with technology, modeling of technology use, collaborative participation, and reflection". TaL builds initial technical and pedagogical understanding through an example activity, while TaD develops integrative TPCK through collaborative lesson-plan design.
requirements: An accessible ML learning platform suited to learners with limited math and computing skills, exemplified by SmileyDiscovery
constraints: The framework targets basic and accessible ML technologies (k-means clustering) before more in-depth ML concepts and methods
target_learning_goals: Technological knowledge of ML concepts and methods
Pedagogical knowledge for ML-supported inquiry-based learning
Positive attitudes toward applying ML in class teaching
examples: Implemented in two 75-minute online classes across two consecutive weeks with 18 K-12 in-service STEM teachers in a teacher education course
key_sources: Jingwan Tang, Xiaofei Zhou, Xiaoyu Wan, Michael Daley, Zhen Bai. (2023). ML4STEM Professional Development Program: Enriching K-12 STEM Teaching with Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00292-4

article_title: Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats
citation: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2
title: Taxonomy of machine learning types by the inputs systems learn from
description: The article organizes machine learning into four types classified by the inputs the system learns from, stating that "Machine learning can be classified according to the inputs that it learns from". The four types are supervised learning (training data plus correct answers), unsupervised learning (learning from a dataset on its own), semi-supervised learning (learning from incomplete data) and reinforcement learning (based on feedback from the environment). Deep learning is presented as a major current research focus within machine learning, itself a subset of artificial intelligence. This taxonomy frames which ML approaches may appear in educational applications.
requirements: Distinguishing the types requires attending to what input data each system learns from, whether correct answers, incomplete data, or environmental feedback
constraints: The article notes most educational ML applications are still being developed so specific algorithms in use are still under consideration
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature of machine learning systems
key_sources: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2

article_title: OCRA, a Mobile Learning Prototype for Understanding Chemistry Concepts
citation: Tenku Putri Norishah Tenku Shariman and Othman Talib. (2017). OCRA, A Mobile Learning Prototype for Understanding Chemistry Concepts. 14th International Conference on Cognition and Exploratory Learning in Digital Age (CELDA 2017). https://www.worldcat.org/isbn/978-989-8533-68-5
title: Mobile learning applications should avoid replicating the classroom direct-instruction model and instead apply more effective instructional models
description: Drawing on Ng and Nicholas (2013), the article argues that preparing mobile learning experiences should not simply reproduce classroom direct instruction. It states that "When preparing mobile learning experiences, it is advisable to avoid replicating the direct instruction model applied in classrooms; instead teachers should strive to apply more effective models to convey instruction". The principle warns against swapping printed worksheets for mobile devices with the expectation that learners will perform better, and the OCRA prototype is presented as an example of a student-centred, interactive alternative.
requirements: Mobile learning designs grounded in current pedagogical approaches rather than mere content delivery
Understanding the use of M-learning tools for mediation
constraints: The article frames this as advice for educators and designers, motivated by the Malaysian context of downloaded offline study notes
target_learners: Net Generation students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Meaningful conceptual understanding rather than rote memorization
examples: OCRA involves students in constructing and applying knowledge through interactive practice rather than delivering online study notes to download
key_sources: Tenku Putri Norishah Tenku Shariman and Othman Talib. (2017). OCRA, A Mobile Learning Prototype for Understanding Chemistry Concepts. 14th International Conference on Cognition and Exploratory Learning in Digital Age (CELDA 2017). https://www.worldcat.org/isbn/978-989-8533-68-5

article_title: 'No words'-Machine-learning classified nonverbal immediacy and its role in connecting teacher self-efficacy with perceived teaching and student interest.
citation: Lazarides, R., Frenkel, J., Petković, U., Göllner, R., & Hellwich, O. (2025). 'No words'—Machine‐learning classified nonverbal immediacy and its role in connecting teacher self‐efficacy with perceived teaching and student interest. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S15–S31. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12732
title: Computer-vision-based machine learning model for assessing teachers' nonverbal immediacy from classroom video
description: A computer vision-based machine learning model that assesses teachers' nonverbal immediacy (NVI) on classroom video data. As the article describes it, 'the architecture of the model comprised submodels assessing relevant behavioural dimensions (gesture intensity, perceived physical distance, facial expression)', plus an overarching main model integrating the individual ratings into an overall NVI score. It was trained on human-rated 30-s video segments from TALIS mathematics lessons, validated with a cross-subject evaluation protocol, and reached an ICC of .690 with human ratings of overall NVI on the validation set before being applied to 623 video segments for the path analyses.
requirements: Human-rated video segments for training the gesture intensity, perceived distance and overall NVI submodels
Video material of sufficient quality for computer vision analysis; four classrooms were excluded for missing or insufficient video
constraints: Body posture ratings showed low interrater reliability (ICC(2,3) = .59) and were excluded from the analyses
The model was developed and applied to frontal-presentation segments without excessive camera movement where the teacher remained fully visible
target_learners: Grades 8-10 mathematics students in German secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Assessment of teachers' nonverbal immediacy as part of studying motivational processes in mathematics instruction
examples: The validated model was applied to analyse an additional 220 30-s segments from the TALIS video corpus, yielding NVI data from a total of 623 video segments for the subsequent path analyses
key_sources: Lazarides, R., Frenkel, J., Petković, U., Göllner, R., & Hellwich, O. (2025). 'No words'—Machine‐learning classified nonverbal immediacy and its role in connecting teacher self‐efficacy with perceived teaching and student interest. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S15–S31. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12732

article_title: Configuration of Mobile Learning Tools to Support Basic Physical Assessment in Nursing Education: Longitudinal Participatory Design Approach.
citation: Egilsdottir H Ösp, Heyn Lena Günterberg, Brembo Espen Andreas, Byermoen Kirsten Røland, Moen Anne, Eide Hilde. (2021). Configuration of Mobile Learning Tools to Support Basic Physical Assessment in Nursing Education: Longitudinal Participatory Design Approach. JMIR mHealth and uHealth. https://doi.org/10.2196/22633
title: General design features for the mLearning suite: accessible, logically structured, smartphone-compatible, usable on the go, with staged access and anonymity options
description: A reusable configuration pattern for mobile learning suites that emerged from the co-design workshops. Students emphasized that "the suite of mLearning tools had to be easily accessible, have a logic structure, be compatible with smartphones, and be usable on the go." Older students recommended limited access for first-year students via an unlockable lock structure, and the possibility of anonymity or avatars if tool use was visible to other students.
requirements: Easily accessible, logically structured, smartphone-compatible, and usable on the go, with links to other relevant web-based resources
constraints: Second- and third-year students recommended limited access for first-year students to avoid overwhelming them with too much information
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning of basic physical assessment skills across learning contexts
examples: A lock in the structure of the suite that could be unlocked by motivated first-year students eager to learn more
key_sources: Egilsdottir H Ösp, Heyn Lena Günterberg, Brembo Espen Andreas, Byermoen Kirsten Røland, Moen Anne, Eide Hilde. (2021). Configuration of Mobile Learning Tools to Support Basic Physical Assessment in Nursing Education: Longitudinal Participatory Design Approach. JMIR mHealth and uHealth. https://doi.org/10.2196/22633

article_title: Successful mLearning Pilot in Senegal: Delivering Family Planning Refresher Training Using Interactive Voice Response and SMS.
citation: Diedhiou A, Gilroy KE, Cox CM, Duncan L, Koumtingue D, Pacqué-Margolis S, Fort A, Settle D, Bailey R. (2015). Successful mLearning Pilot in Senegal: Delivering Family Planning Refresher Training Using Interactive Voice Response and SMS. Global Health: Science and Practice. https://doi.org/10.9745/GHSP-D-14-00220
title: Use mobile phone-based refresher training to complement, not replace, other in-service training approaches
description: The article recommends that mobile refresher training be positioned within a broader training strategy because the medium cannot support all pedagogic objectives. Simple phone-based training "does not permit trainees to interact with the instructor and other participants, perform clinical practice/simulation, or view didactic images". Provision of supplementary written materials and clinical exercises remains essential for certain topics, while guideline updates and rapid information dissemination are well suited to mobile delivery.
requirements: Supplementary written materials and clinical or interactive methods for topics requiring them
constraints: Not appropriate for pedagogic objectives requiring hands-on practice, images, or group interaction
target_learners: in-service health workers in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: knowledge updates and refresher training on clinical guidelines
examples: The authors suggest mobile delivery suits updates on regulations and guidelines and emerging needs such as Ebola prevention requiring rapid dissemination
key_sources: Diedhiou A, Gilroy KE, Cox CM, Duncan L, Koumtingue D, Pacqué-Margolis S, Fort A, Settle D, Bailey R. (2015). Successful mLearning Pilot in Senegal: Delivering Family Planning Refresher Training Using Interactive Voice Response and SMS. Global Health: Science and Practice. https://doi.org/10.9745/GHSP-D-14-00220
